title: Erdős 124 at the boundary: ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1 is exactly an Egyptian fraction

problemStatement.formal: Characterize the boundary face ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1 of the Erdős 124 reciprocal condition (bases dᵢ ≥ 2).
problemStatement.plain: Erdős Problem 124 (weak Burr–Erdős–Graham–Li form) asks when bases d₁,…,d_k ≥ 2 with ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) ≥ 1 make every natural number a sum of integers with only 0/1 digits in base dᵢ. OQ-02 asks what techniques are needed exactly at the boundary ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1.
whyMatters: The parent Erdős 124 entry (Brown's criterion, formally verified by Harmonic's Aristotle, Nov 2025) proves completeness for the closed region ∑ ≥ 1; the boundary is its extreme face and was left as an open question.
Identifying the boundary with Egyptian-fraction decompositions of 1 reframes an opaque reciprocal-sum condition as classical unit-fraction arithmetic.

proven: The substitution eᵢ = dᵢ − 1 turns the boundary ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1 into the Egyptian-fraction equation ∑ 1/eᵢ = 1; the boundary configurations are exactly the unit-fraction decompositions of 1.
Boundary configurations exist with an arbitrary number of bases (Sylvester splitting 1/e = 1/(e+1) + 1/(e(e+1))).
Base-2 rigidity: any boundary configuration that uses d = 2 must be the singleton [2] (ordinary binary).
Concrete witnesses [2], [3,3], [3,4,7], [3,4,8,43] (the last from Sylvester's sequence 2,3,7,43).
open: No new completeness machinery is required: equality is a face of the closed condition the parent already proves complete, so it inherits completeness for free. The parent's deep ≥ 1 completeness theorem is not reproved here.
knownResults.goal: Give the structural answer to OQ-02 and formalize it: the boundary is exactly Egyptian fractions of 1, configurations of every length exist, and the binary case is rigid.

currentState.focus: Verified deliverable: Proofs/Erdos124CompleteSequencesOQ02.lean and gallery entry erdos-124-complete-sequences-oq-02 are complete in main (verified, original badge, 0 sorries, 0 axioms).

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED and verified in main. Proofs/Erdos124CompleteSequencesOQ02.lean (316 lines, 19 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) formalizes the OQ-02 answer: via eᵢ = dᵢ − 1 the Erdős-124 boundary ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1 is exactly an Egyptian-fraction decomposition ∑ 1/eᵢ = 1. The Sylvester splitting gives boundary configurations of every length, and the base-2 case is rigid (forced singleton [2]). Gallery entry present with full meta.json and annotations; badge 'original', status 'verified'. Depends only on standard Mathlib lemmas (List.sum/map, field_simp, Nat.cast_sub) over the foundational axioms.
builtItems: reciSum_eq_egyptSum: the bridge identity reciSum d = egyptSum (d.map (·−1)), proving the boundary face ∑ 1/(dᵢ−1) = 1 equals an Egyptian-fraction decomposition ∑ 1/eᵢ = 1 with eᵢ = dᵢ − 1 (list induction; cons step uses Nat.cast_sub for a ≥ 1).

egyptSum_split + sylvester / sylvester_egyptSum / sylvester_length: the Sylvester splitting 1/e = 1/(e+1) + 1/(e(e+1)) (field_simp) and a recursive construction giving, for each k, an Egyptian decomposition of 1 with exactly k+1 unit fractions and denominators ≥ 1.
exists_boundary_config: for every k ≥ 1 there is a list of k bases, each ≥ 2, with reciSum = 1 — Erdős-124 boundary configurations exist with arbitrarily many bases.

egypt_one_forces_singleton / base_two_forces_singleton: rigidity — any boundary configuration using base d = 2 (unit fraction 1/1) is the singleton [2], i.e. plain binary; no other base fits the unit budget.
Concrete boundary witnesses [2], [3,3], [3,4,7], [3,4,8,43] verified in the Lean file.
Definitions egyptSum and reciSum as list-map-sums over ℚ; gallery entry src/data/proofs/erdos-124-complete-sequences-oq-02 (meta.json + annotations.json).
insights: The boundary is Egyptian fractions: the single substitution eᵢ = dᵢ − 1 converts the opaque reciprocal-sum boundary into the classical ∑ 1/eᵢ = 1, so the 'technique at the boundary' is unit-fraction arithmetic, not new completeness machinery.
Boundary configs exist for every k: Sylvester splitting 1/e = 1/(e+1) + 1/(e(e+1)) trades one unit fraction for two, so the number of bases is completely unconstrained.
Binary is rigid: base d = 2 contributes the full unit fraction 1/1 = 1, leaving zero budget — the only boundary configuration using d = 2 is the singleton [2].

Equality is a face of the closed condition ∑ ≥ 1 the parent already proves complete, so the boundary inherits completeness for free; the new content is combinatorial structure, not a harder analytic theorem.
